own_scenes.family: Segunda ola de Detroit: UR, Plus 8, Carl Craig
own_scenes.desc: Protegido de Derrick May, volvió de Londres en otoño de 1990 con cintas DAT llenas y un sonido años luz por delante de «Elements of Tone»: breakbeats, voces y samples granulosos con un sentido único de la melodía. Como BFC inauguró Fragile, subsello de Transmat, y como Psyche publicó el EP Crackdown (1990), con portadas op art; giró con Rhythim Is Rhythim. Con Damon Booker (DJ en la CJAM de Windsor) fundó Retroactive, que debutó con el recopilatorio Equinox (1990), avance de la siguiente hornada (Urban Tribe de Sherard Ingram, UR, Octave One) cuando KMS y Metroplex estaban casi parados; sacó «Nowhere to Run» de Inertia (Gerald Simpson), «Throw» de Paperclip People y «Never on Sunday» de Octave One. Tras romper con Booker (luego DJ Blackout en Alemania), creó en 1992 Planet E: Innerzone Orchestra, el house de Moodymann, Recloose. Pocos fuera de Detroit dieron a su experimentación el reconocimiento que merecía.

notes.chapter: Cap. 7: Beyond the Dance: The Future Sound of Techno, 1999–?
notes.text: Planet E fue en su momento el sello de Detroit mejor integrado en el mercado estadounidense, gracias a su acuerdo de distribución con Caroline, y su catálogo ecléctico es el modelo que Sicko propone para el futuro.

refs.q: By combining breakbeats, vocals, and noisy, gravelly samples with an uncanny sense of melody and timing, Craig established himself as one of the most innovative artists in the genre.
refs.para: Wedged between the Music Institute on one end and the boom in Detroit party culture a few years later, you had Carl Craig, a former protégé of Derrick May. In the fall of 1990, he returned to Detroit from an extended “residency” in England, bringing with him a new perspective and DATs (digital audio tapes) full of material, including the remains of a failed Sarah Gregory project on Rhythm King. Craig also brought back a sound he had been developing in London, one that jumped light years ahead of the marker set by Plus 8’s first release, “Elements of Tone,” earlier that year. By combining breakbeats, vocals, and noisy, gravelly samples with an uncanny sense of melody and timing, Craig established himself as one of the most innovative artists in the genre. Unfortunately, few outside Detroit would give his experimentation the exposure or recognition it deserved.
